extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent attorneys, and PCT applicants/practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing unity of invention in international (PCT) applications, including rules for intermediate/final products, Markush groupings, overlapping ranges, complementary forms, and examples illustrating a priori and a posteriori unity determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsideration by examiner
rubrics_metrics.description: If developments during search lead to consideration of unity of invention, the question of unity should be reconsidered by the examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reconsideration does not necessarily imply that an objection of lack of unity will be raised; examiner should reassess unity in light of new information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'intermediate' (Rule 13.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'intermediate' is intended to mean intermediate or starting products used to produce final products through a physical or chemical change in which the intermediate loses its identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intermediate includes starting materials that are transformed such that they no longer retain identity in the final product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-condition test for intermediate/final product unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of invention is present between intermediate and final products where the following two conditions are fulfilled: (A) the intermediate and final products have the same essential structural element; and (B) the intermediate and final products are technically interrelated (final product manufactured directly from intermediate or separated only by a small number of intermediates all containing the same essential structural element).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both (A) and (B) must be satisfied for unity based on intermediate/final product relationship. See sub-criteria for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition A — same essential structural element
rubrics_metrics.description: (A) the intermediate and final products have the same essential structural element, meaning either (1) the basic chemical structures are the same, or (2) the chemical structures are technically closely interrelated with the intermediate incorporating an essential structural element into the final product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either identical basic chemical structure or technical close interrelation (essential structural element incorporated) suffices for condition A; examples 8–11 illustrate both situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition B — technical interrelation/manufacturing relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: (B) the intermediate and final products are technically interrelated, meaning the final product is manufactured directly from the intermediate or is separated from it by a small number of intermediates all containing the same essential structural element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manufacturing/precursor relationship must be direct or involve only a small number of intermediates that themselves contain the essential structural element (see Examples 8–11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unknown structures — evidence requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity may be considered present between intermediate and final products of which the structures are not known, provided there is sufficient evidence to conclude that the intermediate and final products are technically closely interrelated (e.g., the intermediate contains the same essential element or incorporates an essential element into the final product).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence can include test data in the specification showing the effect of the intermediate on the final product; absent such evidence, unity on this basis does not exist (see Examples 12 and 13).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepting different intermediates used in different processes
rubrics_metrics.description: It is possible in a single international application to accept different intermediate products used in different processes for the preparation of the final product, provided that they have the same essential structural element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different routes/starting intermediates are acceptable for unity if they share the same essential structural element incorporated into the final product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediate separation by non-new intermediate prohibits unity
rubrics_metrics.description: The intermediate and final products must not be separated, in the process leading from one to the other, by an intermediate that is not new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an intermediate in the chain is old/not new, the intermediate–final unity relationship is broken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple intermediates for different structural parts — lack of unity between intermediates
rubrics_metrics.description: If the same international application claims different intermediates for different structural parts of the final product, unity is not regarded as being present between the intermediates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claiming different intermediates each corresponding to distinct structural parts of the final product breaks unity among those intermediate claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Families mapping requirement for intermediate/final compound families
rubrics_metrics.description: If the intermediate and final products are families of compounds, each intermediate compound must correspond to a compound claimed in the family of the final products; some final products may have no corresponding intermediate compound so families need not be absolutely congruent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-to-one correspondence is expected for claimed family members, but exact congruence of families is not required; see AI Annex B, paragraph (h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Other effects of intermediates do not affect unity
rubrics_metrics.description: As long as unity of invention can be recognized applying the above interpretations, the fact that, besides the ability to be used to produce final products, the intermediates also exhibit other possible effects or activities should not affect the decision on unity of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary activities/properties of intermediates are irrelevant to the intermediate–final unity determination if the required structural/manufacturing relations are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special technical feature concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of special technical features: shared technical features are 'special technical features' if they make a contribution over the prior art. Authorities may differ in determining which features are special technical features on a case-by-case basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a shared feature is a special technical feature depends on contribution over prior art; this determination affects a priori vs a posteriori unity findings (see Examples and paragraph references 10.01–10.10).

rubrics_metrics.name: A priori unity across different claim categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity can exist a priori between different aspects/category of the invention claimed (method, apparatus, product, use etc.) when a common special technical feature is present (e.g., substance X common to method, product, and use claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show method+product+use unity where the common special technical feature (e.g., substance X) is present and contributes over the prior art (see Examples 1–7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Process/product correspondence (inherent product feature)
rubrics_metrics.description: A process claim can correspond to a product claim if the process steps inherently produce the product feature that is the special technical feature of the product claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the product feature is not explicit in the wording of the process claim, disclosure in the description showing the process inherently yields the product characteristic can establish unity (Example 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush/grouping test for alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush grouping (one claim listing alternatives) is acceptable where the alternatives share a significant structural element that is essential to the common property or activity; this shared core provides unity a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The indolyl moiety, thiazole ring, or other shared cores can be the significant structural element. Prior art showing the shared core with the claimed function can destroy unity a posteriori (see Examples 25–29).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of prior art — a posteriori lack of unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity may be lacking a posteriori if the shared technical feature does not make a contribution over the prior art (i.e., is not a special technical feature in view of prior art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art that teaches the shared structure or its function can remove the special technical feature status and break unity (illustrated across examples including Markush cases and overlapping ranges).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial novelty within family members does not necessarily destroy unity
rubrics_metrics.description: If not all members of a claimed family are novel (e.g., some are known), there may nevertheless be unity between a family claim and a specific member claim provided the specific member has the claimed activity that is the special technical feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 7: even if not all compounds in a family are novel, unity can exist if the particular member has the shared activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting first invention to be searched in Markush/non-unity a posteriori cases
rubrics_metrics.description: If unity is lacking a posteriori for a Markush-style claim, Authorities may determine the first named invention searched as the embodiment comprising the first-listed options for each variable (but discretion exists to include sub-genuses depending on circumstances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners consider interdependence of groups, examples, and prior art. Practices differ; sometimes the first embodiment listed is used, other times different groupings are chosen (see Example 25 discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlapping numerical ranges — fact-specific approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of unity for claims containing overlapping ranges requires careful factual consideration; avoid narrow, literal or academic approaches when raising lack of unity objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 20 (manganese ranges) shows that unity between overlapping ranges depends on whether the shared portion is associated with the same technical effect and prior art teachings; prior art can change a priori unity to lack of unity a posteriori.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementary forms — corresponding technical features
rubrics_metrics.description: Complementary forms of an invention (e.g., receiver and transmitter, plug and socket) can have unity when claims include corresponding special technical features present in each complementary form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity is present when a corresponding feature (e.g., time axis expander/compressor) constitutes the special technical feature shared between complementary claims (Examples 21–22).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method-of-screening vs compounds — lack of unity without structural/activity link
rubrics_metrics.description: A screening method claim and claims to compounds identified by that method may lack unity a priori if there is no teaching of a structural element shared by the compounds or a disclosed relationship between structure and activity linking the method to the compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 23: method for identifying antagonists vs diverse compounds X, Y, Z—without structural commonality or explanation of structure–activity relation, there is no single general concept linking the method and compounds, so separate inventions are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative technical solutions to same problem — unity if shared concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Different technical solutions (e.g., mechanical screw vs hydraulic lifting mechanism for a chair) can be united under a single general inventive concept a priori if the common special technical feature (chair with a lifting mechanism) is present; if that concept is known in the art, unity may be lacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity depends on whether the shared concept contributes over prior art; if the broad concept is known, variants may form separate inventions (Example 24).

rubrics_metrics.name: Polynucleotide family unity (common structure + common property)
rubrics_metrics.description: A group of polynucleotides can meet unity if the alternatives share a significant structural element essential to a common property/activity (e.g., expression only in disease hepatocytes) — satisfying both common structure and common property yields unity a priori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 30: SEQ ID NOs 1–10 share a structural element and a disease-expression property; some Offices may view this as a Markush grouping; absence of prior art and disclosure of both requirements supports unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: No unity where claims have unrelated special technical features
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that each contain different unrelated special technical features (e.g., distinct control circuits A and B) do not share unity with one another, though each may share unity with apparatus claims that include the corresponding circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 31: unity exists between a control-circuit claim and an apparatus including that circuit, but not across different, unrelated circuit claims.
